questions.q: A sound wave of frequency 170 Hz travels through air at \(340\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). What is its wavelength?
questions.solution: From the wave equation \(v = f\lambda\): \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\) = 340 ÷ 170 = 2.0 m. Dividing the other way round (0.50 m) is the usual slip.

questions.q: The graph shows a progressive wave at one instant. Points P and Q on the wave are half a wavelength apart. What is the phase difference between them?

figure.alt: Displacement against distance for two wavelengths of a wave. P is at the top of a crest and Q is at the bottom of the next trough, half a wavelength further on.

questions.solution: One whole wavelength is a phase difference of 360° (\(2\pi\) rad). The two points move in antiphase, and half a wavelength is half of a full cycle: 360 ÷ 2 = 180°.

questions.q: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?

options.C: A ripple on the surface of water
options.D: A wave on a stretched string

questions.solution: In a longitudinal wave the particles oscillate along the direction the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound in air is longitudinal. The other three are transverse: their oscillations are at right angles to the direction of travel.

questions.q: Which of these waves can be polarised?
questions.solution: Only transverse waves can be polarised, because only they oscillate at right angles to their direction of travel. Microwaves are electromagnetic, so transverse. Sound, ultrasound and longitudinal seismic waves oscillate along their direction of travel.

questions.q: The graph shows a stationary wave on a string at its two extreme positions. Adjacent nodes are 0.30 m apart, and the string vibrates at 250 Hz. What is the speed of the waves on the string?

figure.alt: The position of the string against distance along it, showing the string at its two extreme positions: three loops, with nodes at 0, 0.30, 0.60 and 0.90 metres and antinodes halfway between them.

questions.solution: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the wavelength is 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 m. Then \(v = f\lambda = 250 \times 0.60 = 150\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Using 0.30 m as the wavelength gives half the true speed.

questions.q: A string of length 0.50 m and mass per unit length \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^{-1}\) is under a tension of 40 N. What is the frequency of its first harmonic?
questions.solution: Wave speed: \(\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{40}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = 200\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). For the first harmonic the string is half a wavelength long: \(f = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\) = 200 ÷ (2 × 0.50) = 200 Hz.

questions.q: How is a stationary wave formed?

options.A: By one progressive wave slowing down until it stops.
options.B: By two waves of different frequencies travelling in the same direction.
options.C: By a wave being absorbed at a boundary.
options.D: By two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions and superposing.

questions.solution: A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency (and similar amplitude) travel in opposite directions and superpose, often a wave and its own reflection. Where they always cancel there are nodes; where they reinforce there are antinodes.

questions.q: What is meant by two coherent sources of waves?

options.A: They have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
options.C: They are the same distance from the screen.
options.D: They emit waves of several different wavelengths.

questions.solution: Coherent sources have the same frequency and keep a constant phase difference. Only then is the interference pattern steady enough to see. They need not have the same amplitude.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.50 mm apart. Fringes are seen on a screen 2.0 m from the slits. What is the fringe spacing?
questions.solution: \(w = \frac{\lambda D}{s} = \frac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 2.0}{0.50 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\), which is 2.4 mm. Every length must be converted to metres first.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. How far from the lens is the real image formed?
questions.solution: Use the thin lens equation, \(\frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f}\). So \(\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{2}{30}\), and v = 15 cm. Adding the two fractions instead of subtracting (7.5 cm) is the usual slip.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating with 300 lines per millimetre. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
questions.solution: Slit spacing: \(d = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{300} = 3.33 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}\). For the first order, \(\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{d} = \frac{600 \times 10^{-9}}{3.33 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.18\), so \(\theta = 10.4^{\circ}\).

questions.q: Monochromatic light passes through a single slit and forms the diffraction pattern shown by the graph. The slit is made narrower. What happens to the central maximum?

figure.alt: Intensity against angle for single-slit diffraction: a tall, wide central maximum, with much lower and narrower maxima on either side.

questions.solution: A narrower slit diffracts the light through a larger angle, so the central maximum spreads out. Less light gets through the slit and it is spread over a bigger area, so the maximum is also dimmer.

questions.q: A ray of light in air meets a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. The refractive index of the glass is 1.50. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.solution: Snell's law with air as medium 1: \(\sin r = \frac{\sin 40^{\circ}}{1.50} = 0.43\), so r = 25°. Dividing the angle itself by 1.50 (27°) is wrong: the law uses sines.

questions.q: What is the critical angle for light travelling from glass of refractive index 1.50 into air?
questions.solution: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary: \(\sin C = \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{1.50} = 0.667\), so C = 42°. Light meeting the boundary at a larger angle is totally internally reflected.

questions.q: The core of an optical fibre is surrounded by cladding. Why must the cladding have a lower refractive index than the core?

options.A: So that light speeds up as it enters the fibre.
options.B: So that light is absorbed at the edge of the core.
options.C: So that light refracts out of the core into the cladding.
options.D: So that light can be totally internally reflected at the boundary between them.

questions.solution: Total internal reflection only happens when light in a material of higher refractive index meets one of lower refractive index, at more than the critical angle. The cladding also protects the core and stops light crossing between fibres that touch.

questions.q: A beam of light delivers a power of 12 W evenly over an area of \(0.30\ \text{m}^{2}\). What is the intensity of the light?
questions.solution: Intensity is power per unit area: \(I = \frac{P}{A} = \frac{12}{0.30} = 40\ \text{W m}^{-2}\). Multiplying instead of dividing (3.6) is the usual slip.
